tier_reason: README Performance section runs the public, automated mimalloc-bench suite (github.com/daanx/mimalloc-bench: bench.sh, build-bench-env.sh, which sets CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS='-march=native') against jemalloc 5.2.1, tcmalloc 2.8.1 and glibc 2.31, stating GCC 9.3.0 / Clang 10.0.0 and CPU models (AMD 5950x, Xeon Cascade Lake c5.18xlarge). The '2.5x faster than jemalloc' sh6bench figure is verbatim prose.

corrections.claimed_speedup: sh6bench: mimalloc "more than 2.5x faster than jemalloc"; larsonN: "quite a bit faster than tcmalloc and jemalloc"; cfrac: "just a tad faster than tcmalloc and jemalloc"; leanN (Lean compiling its own standard library): "a 13% speedup over tcmalloc", which the README extrapolates to "1.6x faster than tcmalloc" if Lean spends 20% of its time in the allocator; xmalloc-testN: mimalloc "outperforms others by a very large margin"; sh8bench: adding object migration makes tcmalloc "10x slower than before" (a tcmalloc-vs-itself remark, not a mimalloc ratio)

notes: Numbers verified verbatim in README (Performance section, 'Last update: 2021-01-30', with a 2026-09-01 'YMMV' note). Removed the unsupported '(mimalloc does not regress)' parenthetical and added the larsonN/cfrac prose; only the sh6bench ratio is a numeric claim vs the jemalloc baseline, leanN is vs tcmalloc. The flags come from the current mimalloc-bench build script, which may differ from the one used in 2021. SVG charts are glyph paths with no extractable glibc numbers, so the caveat is accurate.

tier_reason: The single-threaded run-time tables (cca, gs, sh6bench, smlng vs phkmalloc) are verbatim in the paper, but it is the jemalloc author's own write-up for BSDCan, a practitioner conference that is not a refereed paper venue. Benchmarks are only 'available upon request' and no compiler or flags are given, so these are first-party numbers with partial methodology (C), not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single-threaded programs (mean run time, phkmalloc vs jemalloc, from the paper's tables): cca 77.73s vs 69.37s (~1.12x, derived from page data); gs 42.48s vs 34.24s (~1.24x, derived from page data); sh6bench 6.96s vs 4.50s (~1.55x, derived from page data); smlng 13.89s vs 11.49s (~1.21x, derived from page data); cfrac 11.45s vs 10.55s (~1.09x, derived from page data). Multi-threaded malloc-test (Figure 6, log scale): jemalloc plateaus at roughly 3x10^7 allocations/sec from 4 threads upward (with a dip above 16 threads), while phkmalloc falls below 1x10^5 allocations/sec by 10 threads and was not run beyond 10 threads (on the order of 400x at 10 threads, derived from page data, approximate reading of the log-scale plot)
corrections.caveats: Evidence is jemalloc's own founding paper (Evans, 'A Scalable Concurrent malloc(3) Implementation for FreeBSD', BSDCan 2006), which compares against phkmalloc (FreeBSD's libc malloc at the time) and dlmalloc 2.8.3, not glibc. BSDCan is a practitioner conference, not a peer-reviewed venue, and benchmarks are 'available upon request' with no compiler/flags, so tier C. Numbers are ~20 years old on a dual-dual Opteron 275. dlmalloc beat jemalloc on cfrac, gs and sh6bench. On MySQL super-smack the paper says phkmalloc's median throughput is 'typically about the same as for jemalloc'; jemalloc's gain there is in worst-case variability. No modern jemalloc-vs-glibc numbers were found in the repo (README, TUNING.md have none).

notes: Tier lowered from B to C because a BSDCan paper by the project author is first-party, not peer-reviewed. The Figure 6 reading was corrected: jemalloc plateaus near 3e7, not 2e7, and phkmalloc is below 1e5 at 10 threads, so the gap is about 400x rather than 100x (still approximate). The GitHub license API returns NOASSERTION, but COPYING is 2-clause BSD text with an 'Unless otherwise specified' preamble, so BSD-2-Clause and copyable stand. FreeBSD libc's malloc directory still holds only jemalloc.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed ACM ISMM '19 paper compares against ptmalloc2 from glibc 2.27 in throughput charts (Figs 4-6) and in SPECspeed (Fig 12), where the prose says snmalloc performs 'as well or better than the widely used jemalloc, tcmalloc and glibc's allocator on all benchmarks'. It gives no compiler or flags, so it stays B and cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Figure 5 (producer/consumer malloc-test, random 8-2048B objects, thread sweep): at 64 threads snmalloc ~190M and snmalloc-1mib ~220M allocs/sec vs glibc ~47M (~4x, derived from page data, approximate chart reading). Figure 4 (symmetric workload): at 64 threads snmalloc ~180M vs glibc ~105M allocs/sec (~1.7x, derived from page data, approximate), with tcmalloc/jemalloc/SuperMalloc ahead of snmalloc. Figure 6 (producer/consumer by object size): snmalloc ~570M vs glibc ~110M at 16B (~5x) and ~250M vs ~27M at 1KiB (~9x), with glibc near zero above ~4KiB while snmalloc stays at or above ~120M up to 32KiB (derived from page data, approximate). SPECspeed Integer (Fig 12), verbatim: snmalloc performs "as well or better than the widely used jemalloc, tcmalloc and glibc's allocator on all benchmarks".
corrections.hardware: Micro-benchmarks (Figs 4-10): Ubuntu 18.04 Azure Standard F64s_v2 VM, 64 vCPUs on dual-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8168, 128 GB RAM; SPECspeed suite: Ubuntu 18.04 Azure Standard D3_v2 VM, 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon E5-2673), 14 GB RAM
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2.0k stars; Rust bindings via the snmalloc-rs crate (linked from README)
corrections.caveats: Speedups vs glibc are read off linear-scale throughput charts (Figs 4-6), not stated as ratios in prose, so they are approximate. The only verbatim vs-glibc statement is the SPECspeed 'as well or better' sentence. On the symmetric workload (Fig 4), jemalloc and tcmalloc beat snmalloc. No compiler or flags are given, so B not A. The FreeBSD 12.0 libc integration in the paper was the authors' own experiment (24 Makefile lines) to show ease of adoption; it did not make snmalloc FreeBSD's default malloc, and FreeBSD libc still ships jemalloc. The README says the implementation 'has evolved significantly since the initial paper... most of the meta-data layout has changed', so current performance may differ from the 2019 figures.

notes: Tier B stands, but the record had a false claim: that snmalloc has been FreeBSD libc's default since 12.0 (in stars_or_usage and claimed_speedup). The paper calls FreeBSD libc 'using jemalloc' the baseline, and freebsd-src lib/libc/stdlib/malloc/ contains only jemalloc. The chart numbers (150-200M vs <50M at 64 threads) belong to Figure 5's thread sweep, not the 1KiB-32KiB size sweep (Fig 6b), where glibc is far lower. The hardware split was also wrong: the Xeon 8168 is the CPU of the F64s_v2 VM.

tier_reason: The first-party design doc states verbatim that ptmalloc2 (glibc 2.3) takes ~300ns and TCMalloc ~50ns per small malloc/free pair on a 2.8 GHz P4. There is no benchmark code, compiler, or flags, and a Dec 2024 maintainer note calls the timings obsolete, so C.
notes: Quote and the Dec 2024 editor's warning were verified verbatim in docs/tcmalloc.adoc. The same note adds qualitatively that glibc is 'still being somewhat slower than gperftools' today. The Performance Notes section has no numbers. Metadata (BSD-3-Clause, 8,976 stars, last commit 2026-09-05, not archived) matches.

tier_reason: docs/overview.md only says TCMalloc is an alternative to the glibc/C++ standard library allocator and is 'designed to be more efficient at scale than other implementations'. There are no numbers, and none vs glibc in design.md, temeraire.md, tuning.md, rseq.md, gperftools.md or lifetime-based-allocator.md. Tier D, notable (5.4k stars), so not rejected.

corrections.caveats: No public numeric benchmark of google/tcmalloc vs glibc malloc, std::allocator, or operator new/delete was found in the repo's docs, so this is tier D on the qualitative overview.md claim. Peer-reviewed numeric evidence exists only against TCMalloc's OWN legacy pageheap: Hunter, Kennelly et al., 'Beyond malloc efficiency to fleet efficiency: a hugepage-aware memory allocator' (OSDI 2021). TEMERAIRE improved RPS by 7.7% and cut RAM by 2.4% across 8 applications (abstract). Table 1 averages +5.2% throughput across WSC apps. Fleet IPC rose 1.2%, and pageheap overhead fell from 14.3% to 10.6% (Fig. 15). Redis 6.0.9 gained +0.75% with periodic release off and +0.44% with it on (Intel Skylake Xeon, LLVM cd442157cf -O3, 2000 trials of redis-benchmark with 1,000,000 requests each). That is TCMalloc vs TCMalloc, not vs a listed baseline. google/tcmalloc is the documented successor ('abseil tcmalloc') to gperftools' tcmalloc, whose quoted glibc comparison is recorded under the 'gperftools TCMalloc' entry.

notes: Tier D was correct. I fixed the caveat's OSDI numbers: the '+3.2% average CPU throughput' figure does not appear in the paper. The paper reports +7.7% RPS / -2.4% RAM (abstract), a +5.2% Table 1 average, and +1.2% fleet IPC; the 14.3%->10.6% and Redis +0.75%/+0.44% figures are correct. The input record had no claimed_speedup key; I set it to null.
